standard.title: Diversity of First Nations drama
standard.description: investigate the diversity of drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians, considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have diverse storytelling and performance traditions. They have not yet investigated this diversity systematically or engaged with ICIP rights frameworks in drama contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian drama with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights in drama
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights mean in drama contexts and describe what culturally responsive engagement with First Nations drama looks like in practice
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what ICIP rights are in a drama context; give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations drama looks like
nodes.typical_width: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to drama-making — using cultural stories, developing characters from First Nations contexts, representing historical events
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in drama where ICIP rights were denied — explain what happened, who was harmed, and what a respectful alternative would have been

Use ICIP protocols to reason through whether specific ideas from a cultural source can be used in new drama work — document the reasoning process including 'Whose story is it?' and 'Is this my story to share?'
Explore how drama practitioners can communicate First Nations Australian perspectives on resilience or colonisation respectfully — develop criteria for ethically engaging with this material

response_modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights abstractly without being able to reason through specific drama scenarios — they know permission is needed without being able to work out whose story it is, what counts as cultural expression, or what respectful engagement looks like in practice. Scenario-based scaffolding builds actionable understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The cultural appropriation case study direction requires concrete reasoning about harm, rights and alternatives. The ICIP protocol reasoning direction is also rich — documenting the decision-making process ('Whose story is it?') helps students internalise ethical thinking as a drama practice, not just a compliance check.
success_criteria: Explains what ICIP rights mean in a drama context
Gives at least one specific example of respectful engagement
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind protocols

nodes.label: Investigating diversity of First Nations Australian drama
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian drama practices across contexts with cultural responsiveness
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian drama work or practitioner in depth; explain what makes it culturally significant
nodes.typical_width: Investigate diverse examples of First Nations Australian drama; analyse how practitioners use historical and cultural material to create contemporary theatre; apply ICIP understanding to the investigation
wider: Investigate how contemporary First Nations Australian theatre practitioners use historical and cultural material — analyse how they communicate perspectives on resilience, identity and the impacts of colonisation

Investigate how First Nations Australian drama uses linear and non-linear narrative to explore issues of identity, relationships or empathy — compare with non-First Nations dramatic narrative approaches
Research how diverse First Nations Australian drama reflects the diversity of hundreds of distinct cultural groups — investigate the geographic and cultural breadth of practice

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian drama as a single tradition rather than understanding the enormous diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups, regions and contemporary contexts. Multiple distinct investigation contexts resolve this misconception through genuine breadth.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contemporary theatre direction — how practitioners communicate perspectives on resilience and colonisation — is rich. It surfaces drama as a site of cultural and political work, connecting ICIP principles to active creative practice rather than just historical preservation.
success_criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian drama in genuine depth
Explains cultural significance — not just describes the content

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make ethical choices about how they engage with First Nations Australian drama, applying ICIP protocols when devising, interpreting or performing work.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own drama practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
nodes.typical_width: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice as a devisor, interpreter and performer; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian drama.
wider: Use ICIP protocols to reason through whether ideas from a cultural source can be used in new drama work — document the reasoning process.
Develop criteria for ethically engaging with First Nations Australian perspectives in drama — grounded in specific protocols and the principle of cultural responsiveness.
success_criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical drama practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

response_modes.reason: Applying ICIP protocols to drama requires reasoning through specific questions: whose story is it, is this my story to share, what permission is needed.
